data.title: Middle East Eye: Iran offers to mediate talks between Saudi Arabia and Yemen
data.author: Mera Aladam
data.summary:
Iran offers to mediate talks between Saudi Arabia and Yemen
During an interview with Al Jazeera, Iran's president Masoud Pezeshkian spoke extensively about the conflict in Yemen and its regional repercussions, saying that Iran "doesn't believe Saudi Arabia and Yemen should fight, as they are both Muslims."
He added that Iran would mediate between the two countries: "We are prepared to sit down and help Saudi Arabia and Yemen resolve this issue."
Pezeshkian added that Iran only "empathises"with Yemen, failing to further detail on Iran's support of Ansar Allah, also known as the Houthis. "What happens in Yemen is not related to us," he said.
The conflict in Yemen reignited in July after a fragile ceasefire broke between the Yemeni Saudi-backed government and the Houthis, who control the capital Sanaa. Hundreds of people, mostly fighters, have died as a result of combat and over 100,000 Yemeni were internally displaced.

data.title: Middle East Eye: How the Iran war is squeezing Pakistan, Turkey and Egypt from every direction
data.author: Shady Ibrahim
data.summary:
How the Iran war is squeezing Pakistan, Turkey and Egypt from every direction
Submitted by
Shady Ibrahim
on
Fri, 09/25/2026 - 16:39
Disruptions at Hormuz, Bab al-Mandeb and Suez are only half the story. Pressures are also piling up along their land borders
A ship moves through Egypt’s Suez Canal on 16 April 2025 (Khaled Desouki/AFP)
On
The war on Iran has turned the region’s shipping map into a weapon.
Every extra day of tension around Hormuz, every skirmish near Bab al-Mandeb, every convoy rerouted around the Cape of Good Hope instead of Suez - each adds a small charge to fuel bills, food prices and currencies.
Less discussed is that the three countries absorbing some of the worst of these shocks - Pakistan, Turkey and Egypt - are simultaneously managing tensions on their own borders, with India, Greece and Israel respectively. Instability through Sudan and Libya adds another layer of risk.
Iran, notably, is itself a neighbour to both Turkey and Pakistan. Yet while none of these states is a direct party to the war on Iran, all three are nevertheless fighting on two fronts at once: an economic front at sea, and a security one on land.
The logic is straightforward. Insurers price in the risk of a tanker being struck near Hormuz, where Iran retains significant leverage over passage. Shippers price in the risks of Bab al-Mandeb, after Houthi forces pushed into Dhubab, tightening their grip on the strait. And Suez, one of Egypt’s most reliable sources of foreign currency, has seen its revenues collapse by more than 60 percent.
None of these countries needed a new war to hurt. Pakistan’s inflation had already hit a record 38 percent in 2023, with reserves barely covering two weeks of imports. Egypt’s pound had already fallen from roughly 30 to the dollar towards 50. Turkey’s inflation had scorched past 85 percent in late 2022.
The war reopened wounds barely closed, just as each state was also watching its own borders.

“Our temporary sanctions are not targeted against Israel, but stem from our obligation to not contribute to the unlawful situation ‌of the illegal settlements,” he said in a statement.

Israeli actions 'paving way for total control' over Al-Aqsa, says Hamas
Hamas political bureau member Khaled Meshaal has warned that Israeli actions and measures around Al-Aqsa Mosque are “paving the way for total control and domination over the site”.
Meshaal said the measures included the reported 40-day closure of the mosque, what he described as the “imposition of temporal division” to facilitate incursions by “extremist Jewish groups” and efforts to create “spatial division” by emptying key facilities within the courtyard, according to a statement.
Al-Aqsa “stands at a crossroads”, Meshaal said, and called for steps to protect the site, including what he called a “strategy of resistance and jihad”.
He also urged Arab and Muslim-majority countries to back Palestine and called on Palestinians to keep a “steadfast presence” at the mosque.
The comments come a week after Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu toured tunnels beneath Al-Aqsa Mosque as hundreds of Israeli settlers raided the Jerusalem holy site.

data.title: Middle East Eye: 'No to Israel’s genocidal wars': Hundreds risk arrest outside Labour conference over Palestine Action ban
data.author: Imran Mulla
data.summary:
'No to Israel’s genocidal wars': Hundreds risk arrest outside Labour conference over Palestine Action ban
Submitted by
Imran Mulla
on
Mon, 09/28/2026 - 09:06
The arrests came as protesters called on Burnham to break with the previous government’s approach to Palestine Action
A man is arrested during a protest against the Palestine Action ban in Liverpool, 27 September 2026 (Imran Mulla/Middle East Eye)
Off
Carolyn Gelenter was preparing for her fifth arrest for a terrorist offence.
The 57-year-old daughter of a Holocaust survivor had come outside the Labour Party conference in Liverpool to hold up a placard expressing opposition to genocide and support for the direct action group Palestine Action.
“I feel like this is a great opportunity to reach out to Andy Burnham, who wants to disassociate himself from Keir Starmer’s premiership," Gelenter said.
“There are many of us who are really angry about what’s going on and now’s an opportunity as a new leader of the Labour Party.”
Nearby, a man named Richard prepared to hold up his own placard. He had been arrested several times before for the same offence.
“It’s a bit of a chore,” he said. But it was important to stand up for civil liberties, he added.
Sunday marked the first full day of the Labour conference.
'Continuing the charade of the proscription of Palestine Action is illogical, unsustainable and immoral'

Inside the conference venue, Liverpool’s Exhibition Centre, ministers and MPs were holding panels and giving speeches. Well-dressed men and women filed into the conference clutching copies of the agenda.

Palestinian embassy urges UK action to end Israel’s occupation
The Palestinian embassy in London has called for “urgent action, accountability, and an end to Israel’s unlawful occupation” as it welcomed “recent shifts in UK policy”.
The appeal follows Britain’s announcement of sanctions on goods from illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank. Israel responded by closing the British consulate in occupied East Jerusalem.
In its post on X, the embassy shared footage of diplomat Marwan Yaghi speaking in Liverpool ahead of the Labour Party conference. Arise Festival and Labour Palestine organised the meeting.

data.summary:
Why does the US control Iraq's oil revenues?
Submitted by
Azhar Al-Rubaie
on
Mon, 09/21/2026 - 08:50
A system created after the 2003 invasion was designed to protect Iraq's oil wealth. More than two decades later, it gives Washington significant leverage over Baghdad
A man counts US dollar banknotes at al-Kifah stock market in Baghdad on 27 December 2022 (Ahmad al-Rubaye/AFP)
Off
For more than two decades, Iraq's oil wealth has passed through a financial system centred thousands of miles away in New York.
The arrangement, created after the US-led invasion of Iraq in 2003, was initially designed to protect Iraqi oil revenues from creditors and help fund reconstruction.
Today, it gives Washington significant leverage over Iraq's access to its own dollars, leverage that the US is increasingly using as it pressures Baghdad to curb Iran's influence and the activities of armed groups aligned with Tehran.
The issue came into sharp focus in April, when Washington blocked a shipment of about $500m in cash to Iraq as it pressured the government over Iran-aligned armed groups.
Muayen al-Kadhimi, a former parliamentary Finance Committee member, condemned the decision at the time, calling on the government to end what he described as US dominance over Iraqi funds.
"The US decision to freeze or delay sending Iraq's foreign currency entitlements represents a serious violation of the financial and political sovereignty of the Iraqi state," al-Kadhimi said.
The shipment was later restored, but the episode demonstrated how Iraq's dependence on the US financial system can be used as a political tool.
The arrangement began after the US-led invasion in May 2003, when the Coalition Provisional Authority established the Development Fund for Iraq (DFI) to collect the country's oil revenues and use them for reconstruction and humanitarian needs.
